title: Relatives Are Found By Inherited Traits

scenes.tts: A whale swims in the sea. Its body is shaped like a fish. Yet a whale breathes air with lungs, and it feeds its young milk. Its closest living relatives are hippos. So how do scientists figure out who is related to whom?
scenes.visual: Whale, tuna and hippo chips; a looks-alike link whale to tuna, a question mark link whale to hippo; the question appears.
scenes.narration: A whale swims in the sea. Its body is shaped like a fish. Yet a whale breathes air with lungs, and it feeds its young milk. Its closest living relatives are hippos. So how do scientists figure out who is related to whom?

scenes.tts: Scientists group living things by how they are related. This is called classification. They do not group by looks, home, or diet. Those can match in animals that are not close relatives. Instead, they compare inherited evidence: body parts, embryos, fossils, and DNA. They trust a grouping most when the kinds of evidence agree.
scenes.visual: Classification label; looks, home, diet chips crossed out; four evidence chips appear and a bracket labelled agree closes over them.
scenes.narration: Scientists group living things by how they are related. This is called classification. They do not group by looks, home, or diet. Those can match in animals that are not close relatives. Instead, they compare inherited evidence: body parts, embryos, fossils, and DNA. They trust a grouping most when the kinds of evidence agree.

scenes.tts: Look at the front limb of a human, a bat, and a whale. A hand grasps, a wing flies, a flipper steers. Yet each has one upper arm bone, two forearm bones, wrist bones, and finger bones. Parts built the same way are called homologous structures. They were inherited from a common ancestor.
scenes.visual: Three columns of labelled blocks, matching blocks the same colour; a common ancestor chip with arrows to the three columns.
scenes.narration: Look at the front limb of a human, a bat, and a whale. A hand grasps, a wing flies, a flipper steers. Yet each has one upper arm bone, two forearm bones, wrist bones, and finger bones. Parts built the same way are called homologous structures. They were inherited from a common ancestor.

scenes.tts: Embryos can share parts that adults lose. Early fish, chick, and human embryos all have a tail. They also have a row of folds in the neck, called pharyngeal arches. In fish, several arches go on to support gills. In humans, they become parts of the jaw, ear, and throat. Human embryos do not turn into fish first.
scenes.visual: Three embryo blocks each with tail and arches blocks; the arches in fish become gills, in human become jaw, ear, throat.

scenes.tts: A cladogram is a branching diagram. It shows the order in which groups split from common ancestors. It is built from shared derived characteristics. That is a trait that first appeared in one ancestor and passed to its descendants. Hair is one. Mammals share it, and fish and frogs do not.
scenes.visual: A branch point grows into two branches; the hair mark sits on the mammal branch; the node is labelled common ancestor.

scenes.tts: Now place the whale. Lungs and milk put it with the mammals, not the fish. Fossil whales with legs, embryos, and DNA it shares with hippos all point the same way. The fishlike shape fits life in water. Keep this rule: judge relatives by inherited traits, not by looks.
